newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin vows to press for Karabakh peace.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin vows to press for Karabakh peace.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said Russia and oil-rich Azerbaijan had solved most bilateral problems on Thursday, and he vowed to join Paris and Washington in helping to end the long-running Nagorno-Karabakh conflict.

Azeri President Haydar Aliyev's visit has been seen as something of a fence-mending exercise. Ties between Moscow and Baku have been soured by mutual recriminations ranging from trade hitches to accusations they helped each other's rebels.
"There are no more unresolved problems between Russia and Azerbaijan," Yeltsin told a wider meeting after about 90 minutes of Kremlin talks with Aliyev. "We have solved them."

But Yeltsin added ministers still had to iron out some differences concerning the status of the Caspian Sea, the planned pipeline route through Russia to deliver oil to Black Sea ports and a railway linking the two ex-Soviet republics.

Yeltsin vowed to step up peace-making efforts on Nagorno-Karabakh, an enclave mainly populated by Armenians but inside Azerbaijan. Russia, France, and the United States co-chair negotiations between the sides.

He said France and the United States had agreed to join him in a renewed and concerted effort to steer Azeri and Armenian leaders towards a lasting settlement. There has been a truce for three years but there is still some shooting. Thousands died during the height of the war in the late 1980s.

"I have agreed with U.S. President Bill Clinton and French President Jacques Chirac that we will get together finally to find a way to make the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia sit at the negotiating table and sign an agreement or a treaty," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
He did not say when and where the talks would be held.

Yeltsin, Clinton and Chirac, who discussed the problem during a world summit in the U.S. city of Denver last month, have proposed giving Karabakh wide autonomy within Azerbaijan, but the Karabakh Armenians have been unenthusiastic.

During their Kremlin talks, Yeltsin and Aliyev signed a series of bilateral documents including an updated version of a 1992 friendship treaty in which they vowed not to allow their territories to be used for activities against the other.

Aliyev, a 74-year-old veteran of the Soviet ruling Politburo who helped oust Yeltsin from the Communist Party leadership in 1987, made little comment. It was not clear whether he shared Yeltsin's optimistic view of their talks.
Baku was outraged by reports leaked by Russian deputies that Moscow had supplied arms worth nearly $1 billion to Armenia.
Interfax quoted Aliyev as saying on his arrival to Moscow he was going to raise this with Yeltsin and demand that the weapons, which Baku sees as a threat to its security, are repatriated.
For their part, Russian officials have accused Azerbaijan of allowing weapons and money to flow to pro-independence rebels from its breakaway region of Chechnya during a 21-month war.
Russia temporarily cut rail and roads links with Azerbaijan during the Chechen war, which ended last August.

Aliyev has denied helping the Chechens and blames Moscow for offering refuge to his political foes, such as a former Azeri president, Ayaz Mutalibov, who is wanted by Baku's security services for allegedly plotting a coup d'etat.

"Both sides denounce separatism and promise to ban and prosecute on their territories any organisations whose activities are aimed at the other's independence and territorial integrity," the treaty said, according to Itar-Tass news agency.
The moves to heal political ties come as Moscow and Baku engage in tough economic talks on rights for the oil-rich Caspian sea shelf and terms for transporting Azeri oil.
Aliyev's office said on Tuesday Azerbaijan and Russian oil giant LUKoil would sign a deal this week on jointly developing the Yalama oil field in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea.
LUKoil President Vagit Alekperov said in May the offshore field is estimated to hold at least 50 million tonnes of crude.
Aliyev's visit is also aimed at lifting the last obstacles to an accord on the transit of Azeri oil through Chechnya.
Baku has accused Russia of lagging behind in implementing the deal on the pipeline, which is due to carry the first oil from an $8 billion international consortium by October.
